title: Neural Dynamics Decoding Using Hierarchical Clustering and Multivariate Pattern Analysis
author: Li, Hasegawa, et al.

steps.title: Generate TFR for clustering
steps.instruction: Configure all parameters for the time‑frequency analysis of the odd‑trial dataset and run the script P1_Averaging_TFR_div00.m to create the structure TFR_trldata for hierarchical clustering.

substeps.instruction: Set input_path to the folder containing the data, e.g., 'D:\sample_data'.
Set trldata_name = 'trldata_odd.mat' (the odd‑numbered trials file).
Set slct_channel = {'all'} to analyse all channels.
Set savename_postfix = '_odd' so the output filename is identifiable.
Define the time of interest: toi = -1.0:0.05:2.0 (from –1 s to 2 s in 50 ms steps).
Define the frequencies of interest: foi = 1:1:80 (1 Hz to 80 Hz in 1 Hz steps).
Select the TFR calculation method: TFRMethod = 1 (Morlet wavelet).
Set length_timwin = 0.5 s (length of the time window used by the analysis).
Set flgTFRHz = 1 to normalise power by 1/Hz.
Set flgFbAveraging = 0 so that power is calculated for every frequency (no band averaging).

Run the MATLAB script P1_Averaging_TFR_div00.m; the script will call ft_freqanalysis with the above settings, import trldata_odd.mat, compute the TFR, and save the resulting structure as TFR_trldata in the ‘processed’ subfolder. The filename will contain ‘div00’ and the postfix ‘_odd’ (e.g., TFR_trldata_div00_odd.mat).
Pause here if desired after the TFR file has been saved.

steps.title: Generate band‑averaged TFR for decoding
steps.instruction: Configure parameters for a band‑averaged time‑frequency analysis of the even‑trial dataset and run the script P3_Averaging_TFR_div01.m to produce a TFR structure that will be used for neural decoding.

substeps.instruction: Set input_path to the folder containing the data (same as in Step 1).
Set trldata_name = 'trldata_even.mat' (the even‑numbered trials file, independent from the clustering data).
Set savename_postfix = '_even' to label the output file.
Set flgFbAveraging = 1 to enable averaging of power across predefined frequency bands.
Define freqband as a cell array of frequency‑band vectors, e.g., {4:7, 8:10, 11:21, 22:32, 33:80}. Replace these example ranges with the bands derived from the dendrogram in the clustering step.

Run the MATLAB script P3_Averaging_TFR_div01.m; it will perform the same ft_freqanalysis as in Step 1, then average power within each band defined in freqband, and save the result as TFR_trldata in the ‘processed’ folder. The filename will contain ‘div01’ and the postfix ‘_even’ (e.g., TFR_trldata_div01_even.mat).
Pause here if desired after the band‑averaged TFR file has been saved.

steps.title: Perform MVPA time‑series decoding
steps.instruction: Configure all MVPA parameters and run the script P4_TC_decoding.m to decode stimulus classes from the band‑averaged TFR and obtain statistical significance via bootstrap.

substeps.instruction: Set input_path to the folder where the band‑averaged TFR file from Step 2 resides (e.g., 'D:\sample_data').
Set TFR_trldata_name = 'TFR_trldata_div01_even' (the name without the .mat extension).
Set output_postfix = '_even' to label decoding output files.
Define slct_time_point.training = [1:2:61] (indices of time points used for training).
Define slct_time_point.test = [1:2:61] (indices of time points used for testing; same as training in the example).
Set num_fold = 10 for 10‑fold cross‑validation.
Set flg_bootstrap = 1 to perform bootstrap resampling for statistical testing.
Set ntimes_iter = 1000 (number of bootstrap iterations).
Set num_channel = 64 (number of channels to include in decoding).
Set slct_freqb = [1:5] (indices of the frequency bands defined in Step 2 to be decoded).
Define class_stim matrix:
Adjust the above rows to match the experimental class definitions of your data.
Set svm_solver = 2 to use LibLinear (1 would select LIBSVM).
Set decoding_option = '-s 2 -q -c 0.001' (LibLinear options; modify as needed for your data).

Run the MATLAB script P4_TC_decoding.m; the script will load the TFR structure, select data according to the specified channels, frequency bands, and time points, build feature vectors and labels, perform n‑fold cross‑validation, train an SVM for each fold and time point, compute decoding accuracy, and evaluate significance using the bootstrap procedure (or a binomial test if flg_bootstrap = 0).

The script saves a MATLAB structure named decoding_results in a ‘decoding’ subfolder of input_path. decoding_results contains rate_ave (average accuracy matrix) and rate_ave_pw (per‑class accuracy matrix).
Pause here after decoding_results has been saved; the analysis may take several hours to days.

description: Traditional methods for dividing the frequency spectrum in neural data analysis often have limitations. Conventional techniques typically use predefined bands such as delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (30–100 Hz), based on historical and empirical observations. However, the definitions of these band ranges vary among researchers, leading to confusion and potential inconsistencies in data interpretation.2 While frequency bands are thought to be roughly conserved across mammalian species despite differences in brain size,3 non-negligible variability exists between individuals.4 Moreover, task conditions can influence frequency-specific effects. For example, effects traditionally associated with the alpha band may appear beyond conventional frequency ranges,5 or shifts in the gamma band frequency range may occur.6 These observations suggest that fixed band divisions may not adequately capture the complexity of neural oscillatory activity, potentially leading to a loss of important information and reduced accuracy in neural decoding. To address these limitations, this protocol uses hierarchical clustering to inform the definition of frequency bands based on the inherent structure of the data. The protocol first derives a hierarchical cluster structure based on similarities within the data itself to overcome the constraints of conventional fixed band divisions. This resulting structure then guides subsequent manual refinement, enabling informed decisions about the final band boundaries. Leveraging clustering results to guide manual adjustments helps reveal novel and potentially more functionally relevant frequency bands that might be overlooked by conventional methods.
